flashcards.q: Why can't prompt injection be fixed the way SQL injection was fixed?
flashcards.a: SQL has a real grammar; parameterization compiles query structure before user data is bound, so the parser can't reinterpret data as syntax. Natural language has no equivalent grammar — there's no placeholder to bind around, so instructions and data always share one channel.

flashcards.q: Direct vs indirect prompt injection — define both.
flashcards.a: Direct: the user themselves types the attack into their own input. Indirect: the attack arrives embedded in content the model reads later — a web page, a RAG document, a tool's error string, even a filename.

flashcards.q: Indirect vs direct injection success rate from the 2026 Gray Swan/NIST red-team analysis?
flashcards.a: Indirect attacks succeeded 27.1% of the time vs 5.7% for direct attacks, across 1.8M submitted attacks against 22 frontier agents.

flashcards.q: What are the three legs of Simon Willison's lethal trifecta?
flashcards.a: Access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. All three present means an attacker who controls any untrusted content the agent reads can potentially exfiltrate the private data.

flashcards.q: What's the primary fix once you identify a lethal trifecta in an agent design?
flashcards.a: Remove one leg (make browsing read-only with no rendering, scope away private-data access from the session, or gate external communication behind approval) rather than relying on detecting the injection harder.

flashcards.q: What is LLM01 in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, and how many consecutive editions has it held that spot?
flashcards.a: Prompt Injection — LLM01 for the third consecutive edition. Found in 87% of enterprise-pentested LLM apps in 2025-2026.

flashcards.q: What are the three new/changed categories in the OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 edition vs the prior list?
flashcards.a: System Prompt Leakage (LLM07) and Vector and Embedding Weaknesses (LLM08) are new; Unbounded Consumption (LLM10) expanded from Model Denial of Service; Misinformation (LLM09) absorbed the old Overreliance category.

flashcards.q: What does LLM06 Excessive Agency mean concretely for an agent?
flashcards.a: The agent has more functionality, permissions, or autonomy than its task requires — e.g. a calendar assistant given a generic delete-any-event tool when it only ever needs to create events on the requesting user's own calendar.

flashcards.q: Name two risk categories from the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (Dec 2025) not covered by the original LLM Top 10.
flashcards.a: Agent behavior hijacking and tool misuse/exploitation (also: identity and privilege abuse, and memory/context poisoning).

flashcards.q: Why is a system-prompt rule like 'never delete records without confirmation' not a security control?
flashcards.a: It's advisory text in the same channel an attacker's injected content can also write to, so it competes with the attack on equal footing instead of from a privileged position. A permission engine evaluated as code, which the model cannot influence, is the actual control.

flashcards.q: Are MCP tool annotation hints (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) an enforcement mechanism?
flashcards.a: No. They're self-asserted by the tool server and unenforced — useful as inputs to a permission engine's decision, not a substitute for one.

flashcards.q: What's the observable trace symptom of a successful prompt injection?
flashcards.a: A tool call to a target, recipient, or destination that was never present in the user's own request, appearing immediately downstream of a step that ingested untrusted content (a document read or a web fetch).

flashcards.q: Name two indirect-injection benchmarks used to measure agent injection resistance, with their scale.
flashcards.a: AgentDojo (97 realistic tasks, 629 security test cases, NeurIPS 2024) and AgentHarm (110 malicious tasks, 440 with augmentations, 11 harm categories).

flashcards.q: Does a more capable/larger model resist prompt injection better?
flashcards.a: No clear correlation was found between model capability or size and injection robustness in NIST's 2026 red-team analysis. Model upgrades don't fix this; harness and architecture changes do.

flashcards.q: What made the GitLab Duo Chatbot exploit a textbook lethal trifecta?
flashcards.a: It could ingest a public project's text containing rogue instructions (untrusted content), had access to private repository information (private data), and could render attacker-supplied content/links (external communication) — all three legs simultaneously live.
